doc.title: Joe LaBarbera interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 15, 2021

title: Listening to Bill Evans, Miles and Coltrane instead of pop
summary: As teens the brothers were captivated by Evans, Miles and Coltrane records, played on a portable player in the basement, with father singing along to Mulligan.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Did the music of the pop world have much influence on your listening habits or did you feel desire to get into, well I’ll call it rock music?

It just, you know we heard Bill Evans and Miles and Coltrane when we were in our early teens. I mean that just captivated us. How could we compare that with what was being played on the radio at that time? We’re talking 1960 now. There really is no comparison. I have grown to love the pop music from that era now. I listen to it now. I’m playing catch-up with that and really enjoying it. At the time, Monk, I had no use for it whatsoever.

When you were listening to Bill Evans and Cannonball and all that, did you sense the song form and what the band was doing to make a seven minute performance into a cohesive listenable piece of music?

Not that early on. All I know is that we were completely engaged from the second that needle hit the grooves of the LP until the side was over, it was just like that music completely captivated us and drew us in and didn’t release us until it was finished.
Okay I’m getting a picture in my head of the three of you in one of your bedrooms with that LP going and like, “Oh, listen to that, listen to that, oh.”

Close. It was in the basement or it was in the kitchen. It was a portable job you know, real small, one and a half watts of power, and we would take that everywhere. So we would be listening in the basement constantly and then we’d take it upstairs and play it during dinner and our parents were just fine you know. My father started singing along with Gerry Mulligan after a while.
I guess he was the first Joe LaBarbera.
